1.1:
Where the statues came from: al-Bukhari reports from Ibn Abbas (quoted by Ibn Kathir) that Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr were named after righteous men of Nuh's people. When they died, Satan prompted their people to set up statues in their gathering places, named after them; the statues were not worshipped until that generation had died and the knowledge was lost. Ibn Abbas adds that these idols later turned up among the Arab tribes.

The Shia narrations name other idols that Nuh's people set up, and do not link them to the five names in the Qur'an.
1.2: Ibn Jarir (in the commentary) reports from Muhammad bin Qays that the first statues were made with a good intention: 'if we make images of them, it will increase our desire to worship when we remember them'. Later generations were told the statues brought rain, and worshipped them. The game uses this to show how a small step away from Allah can grow over the years.
1.3: Ask your child: how can something start as a good idea and end up wrong? Remembering good people is good; worshipping them is not.
1.4: The five names are in the Qur'an itself (71:23): the chiefs told the people not to give up their gods.
1.5: Walk around your home together and name things: who made the cup? Who made the rain? Everything people make, they make from what Allah made.
1.6: Ask: who do we ask when we need help? Allah hears every prayer, even a whispered one.
2.1: Nuh's name: the Shia narrations in the Shia narrations give him an earlier name, 'Abd al-Ghaffar (Imam al-Sadiq) or Sakar (Imam al-Rida), and say he was called Nuh, from nawh, mourning, because he grieved so much over his people (or, in another narration, over himself). The commentary on these verses does not discuss the name.
2.2: Ask: what does it mean to warn someone? When have you warned a friend about something dangerous?
2.3: Ask your child to say Nuh's message in their own words.
2.4: The 950 years are in the Qur'an (29:14). The narrations differ on his whole lifespan: in the Shia narrations, Imam al-Sadiq gives about 2,500 years in all, others different figures. The game keeps to the Qur'an's number.
2.5: Count together by hundreds: one hundred, two hundred... up to nine hundred, and then fifty more. Ask: how long is that compared to your age?
3.1: Ask: when is a good time to talk to someone about Allah? Any time, kindly.
3.2: Ask: what do you do at night before you sleep? Some families read a short surah or say a dua together.
3.3: Talk about the difference between speaking to a crowd and talking with one friend. Which is easier for you?
3.4: After the game, ask: Nuh called his people in the day and at night. What can we do both day and night? (Remember Allah, be kind.)
3.5: The fingers in the ears and the clothes over the heads are 71:7: Nuh says they did it 'every time I call them, so that You may forgive them'.
3.6: Ask: how does it feel when someone won't listen to you? What did Nuh do? He kept going.
4.1: This is 71:10-12: Nuh tells his people that if they ask their Lord for forgiveness, He will send rain, and give them wealth, sons, gardens and rivers.
4.2: Ask: what happens to plants when it doesn't rain? Who sends the rain?
4.3: Ask: what are the gifts you are most thankful for? Make a list together.
4.4: If you can, look at the moon and the sky together tonight. Say subhanallah.
4.5: Plant a seed together and watch it grow: the verse says Allah made us grow from the earth like a plant (71:17).
4.6: Ask your child to explain each match: what does the rain give us? What does the moon give us?
5.1: The chiefs' words are 11:27; Nuh's answer that he asks no reward and will not drive the believers away is 11:29-31.
5.2: Ask: has anyone ever been left out of a game? How did they feel? What could you do?
5.3: Ask: why do some people help without wanting anything back? Nuh did his work for Allah alone.
5.4: Make a family plan: one way to make someone new feel welcome this week.
5.5: Ask: who do you know who welcomes everyone? What do they do?
6.1: The commentary explains that this revelation (11:36) came after Nuh had called on Allah for help, 'I am defeated: help me!' (54:10), and asked that no disbeliever be left on the earth (71:26). The game leaves Nuh's prayer against his people for older children.
6.2: Ask: what would you need to build a huge ship? (Wood, nails, tools, help, patience.)
6.3:
The commentary explains 'with Our revelation' as 'We will teach you what to do'.

You may hear the Ark's size: The commentary quotes Muhammad bin Ishaq, 'from the Torah', that it was of Indian teak, eighty cubits long and fifty wide, thirty high, with three decks: animals at the bottom, people in the middle, birds at the top. It comes from the People of the Book, not from the Qur'an or hadith.

The Shia narrations say the Ark was built at the place of the mosque of Kufa, and give thirty, eighty or a hundred years for the building; those narrations reject the figure of five hundred.
6.4: Build a little boat together from paper, a plastic bottle or wood, and see if it floats.
6.5: Ask: why do you think the Qur'an mentions the planks and the nails? Allah's help and Nuh's hard work went together.
6.6: Count the nails together as your child taps.
7.1: The chiefs' mockery and Nuh's answer are 11:38-39. The commentary: they laughed because they did not believe his warning that they would drown.
7.2: Ask: what can you say when someone laughs at you for doing the right thing?
7.3: Ask: have you ever wanted to give up? What helped you keep going?
7.4: Ask: what is something that takes a long time to finish? A puzzle, a drawing, learning a surah?
7.5: Ask your child to hold the hammer as long as they can. Then talk about patience: waiting calmly and keeping on.
8.1: 'The oven gushed forth' (11:40): Ibn Abbas, in the commentary, says the 'oven' (tannur) is the face of the earth, which became springs of water, until water gushed even from the places of fire; The commentary calls this the view of most early and later scholars. The Shia narrations place it in an oven in the mosque of Kufa, which Nuh had sealed and opened when the Ark was finished. The game says only that water burst up even where fires had burned.
8.2: Ask: what does rain sound like? Listen together next time it rains, and say a dua for good rain.
8.3:
The commentary: a pair of every kind of creature with a soul; 'some said' plants too. 'It has also been said' that the parrot was the first bird to board and the donkey the last animal.

You may hear a story, in the Shia narrations of Hayat al-Qulub, that the donkey stopped at the door because Iblis was holding on to it, and both came in. The game leaves this out.
8.4: Name each animal pair and the sound it makes.
8.5: Ask: which animal would you most like to have looked after on the Ark?
8.6:
About eighty believers: Ibn Abbas in the commentary ('eighty people including their women') and Imam al-Rida in the Shia narrations ('eighty believers'). Another Shia narration, from Imam al-Baqir, says only eight believed; the book reconciles the two.

Not everyone in Nuh's family believed: The commentary names his son and his wife among those who did not board, and the Qur'an gives Nuh's wife as an example of a disbeliever married to a righteous man (66:10).
9.1: 11:41. Nuh's words 'bismillahi majraha wa mursaha' (in the name of Allah it sails and comes to rest) are said by some Muslims when they set off on a journey. The prayer on page 9.4 is 23:28-29.
9.2: Next time you set off in a car or bus, say bismillah together, and if you like, the whole phrase: bismillahi majraha wa mursaha.
9.3: Ask: what other times do we say bismillah? (Eating, starting something, going out.)
9.4: Ask: what are you thankful for today? Say al-hamdu lillah together.
9.5: Say the prayer together line by line before tapping.
10.1:
The game tells chapter 10 gently: no picture shows anyone in the water, and it stops at 'the waves came between them'. The verse goes on to say that the son was among the drowned (11:43).

The son's name: The commentary gives it as Yam. The Shia narrations do not name him. Both treat him as Nuh's own son. The game says only 'his son'.
10.2: Hold your child's hand while they hold the Ark steady. Ask: who keeps us safe in a storm?
10.3: Ask: why did Nuh call his son? Because he loved him and wanted him safe.
10.4: Ask gently: is a mountain stronger than Allah's command? What is the only real safety?
10.5: This is a sad part of the story. If your child is upset, hold them and talk about it: Nuh loved his son very much.
10.6: Ask your child: who keeps us safe? Make a short dua for safety together.
10.7: 'He was not one of your family' (11:46): The Shia narrations explain it as 'not of the household of believers', since those who obey Nuh are counted as his household, and holds that he was Nuh's own son. The game uses the verse's own words: what he did was not right.
10.8: Ask: what can we do when we don't understand why something happened? (Trust Allah, ask for help, be patient.)
11.1: Ask: how do you think the people in the Ark felt when the sun came out?
11.2: Ask your child to rub the water away slowly, and talk about the moment the storm ended.
11.3: Al-Judi: Mujahid (in the commentary) says it is a mountain in al-Jazira, northern Mesopotamia; Qatada says the Ark rested on it for a month, and that early Muslims could still see it. The Shia narrations call it 'a great mountain in Mosul'. A Shia narration from Imam al-Sadiq says the Ark first went seven times around the Ka'ba.
11.4: The humble mountain: Mujahid (in the commentary) says that on the day of the flood all the mountains raised themselves up, but al-Judi humbled itself before Allah, so the Ark came to rest on it. The Shia narrations tell the same from Imam Musa al-Kazim.
11.5: Ask: what does it mean to be humble? Can you think of a humble person you know?
11.6: Ask: what would you do first if you came out after a long storm?
11.7: 'He was truly a thankful servant' is 17:3. Imam Zayn al-Abidin is reported in the Shia narrations to have said that people learned 'thankfulness from Nuh', and the same book says Nuh was called thankful for a prayer of thanks he said every morning and evening.
11.8: This prayer is 71:28: rabbighfir li wa li walidayya wa li man dakhala baytiya mu'minan wa lil-mu'minina wal-mu'minat. A good one to learn together.
11.9: Learn Nuh's prayer together, a line a day. It includes a prayer for parents.
11.10: Ask your child to tell the whole story of Nuh in their own words. Which part did they like best?
